meta_title: The Rapture and the Second Coming: Questions and Answers | Bible Insight
meta_desc: A careful, text-based look at the pretribulation rapture: four views compared, seven lines of biblical evidence, answers to eight common objections, with theological notes and a bibliography.
title: The Rapture and the Second Coming
subtitle: When will the Lord come for His people?
lead: This section was not written to calculate dates or to frighten anyone. It was written to examine from Scripture the "blessed hope" the Bible promises, and to help us live watchfully today. Bible Insight teaches the pretribulation rapture as the view that best fits the biblical text. We also gladly honor believers who hold other views as brothers and sisters waiting for the same Lord.
updated: Written November 2026 · Bible Insight editorial team

body.p: The word "rapture" means being "caught up." It refers to the event in which the Lord descends into the air: believers who have died in Christ are raised first, and believers who are still alive are changed in body and caught up together with them to meet the Lord.

The Greek verb behind "caught up" is **harpazō (ἁρπάζω)**, meaning to seize suddenly and forcibly.[^1] The Latin Vulgate rendered it with a form of rapio (rapiemur), and from that Latin root comes the English word "rapture." The term is a theological label for exactly what this verse describes.

Paul calls this a "mystery," that is, a truth not revealed in the Old Testament but now made known. It is the promise that one generation of believers will be changed in an instant without passing through death.

Most Bible-believing scholars agree that there will be a rapture. They differ on **when** it happens. The reference point is Daniel's seventieth week, the seven-year Tribulation that comes just before the Lord's return to the earth.[^2]

body.note: All four views are differences of interpretation within historic orthodox faith. The timing of the rapture is not a condition of salvation. This section explains why we hold the pretribulation view, but it does not condemn scholars or believers who hold another.[^3]

body.h3: ① The Lord may come at any time — imminence

body.p: The New Testament does not tell believers to wait by counting signs. It tells them to wait for a Lord who may come today. This is called **imminence**. If the rapture came at the end of the Tribulation, believers could watch the Antichrist appear and the seven years unfold, and estimate the date. That would not fit the words "in such an hour as ye think not."[^4]

body.h3: ② The church is not appointed to wrath

body.p: While explaining "the day of the Lord" to the Thessalonians (1 Thess. 5:1–3), Paul says that believers are not appointed to that wrath. In Revelation, already at the opening of the sixth seal the people of the earth cry out, "the great day of his wrath is come" (Rev. 6:16–17), and with the seven last plagues "is filled up the wrath of God" (Rev. 15:1). If the Tribulation is thus a period in which God's wrath falls on the earth, the promise of deliverance from that wrath fits best with being removed from that period.

body.h3: ③ Kept from the hour of trial

body.p: "Keep thee from" translates the Greek **tēreō ek (τηρέω ἐκ)**, "to keep out of." The Lord does not say He will bring the church through the trial. He says He will keep it from the very "hour" of trial that is coming upon the whole world.[^5] The ones being tested are "them that dwell upon the earth," who are distinguished from a church whose citizenship is in heaven.

body.h3: ④ Rescue comes before judgment — the days of Lot

body.p: The Lord compared the last days to the days of Lot. The angel says, "I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither." Removing the righteous first and then judging is the way God works (compare 2 Pet. 2:6–9).

body.h3: ⑤ Watch, so that you may escape all these things

body.p: The Lord did not only say "endure" the coming troubles. He said to pray to be counted worthy to "escape" them, and He placed at the end the promise of standing "before the Son of man."

body.h3: ⑥ The Bridegroom takes the bride to the Father's house

body.p: The Lord promised to prepare a place and then to "come again, and receive you unto myself." The direction of this promise is not the earth but "my Father's house." In Jewish wedding custom, the bridegroom first prepared a room in his father's house and then came to bring his bride home. The rapture is the Bridegroom coming for His bride; the coming to the earth is the King appearing with His bride.

body.h3: ⑦ The coming in the air and the coming to the earth are different scenes

head: Rapture (coming in the air)
Coming to the earth
rows: The air — believers rise to meet Him (1 Thess. 4:17)
The earth — His feet stand on the Mount of Olives (Zech. 14:4)
He comes with His saints (Col. 3:4; Rev. 19:14)
After the signs of the Tribulation (Matt. 24:29–30)

body.p: If these are merged into one event, the texts collide. Seen as two phases, each text finds its place. It is also often noted that from Revelation 4 through 19, while the events on earth are described, the word "church" does not appear even once.[^6]

qa.q: In Matthew 24:31 the angels gather "the elect." Isn't that the rapture?

a.p: This scene takes place "immediately after the tribulation of those days" (v. 29). The ones who gather are angels, and the gathering is "from one end of heaven to the other." In 1 Thessalonians 4, the Lord Himself comes and believers are caught up "in the air." The Olivet Discourse (Matt. 24) is set against the background of Judea, the temple and the Sabbath, so the "elect" here are most naturally understood as Israel and the believers who pass through the Tribulation (compare Isa. 27:12–13).[^7]

qa.q: Isn't "the last trump" (1 Cor. 15:52) the seventh trumpet of Revelation?

a.p: First Corinthians was written about forty years before Revelation. The Corinthian believers could not have known the order of trumpets in a book not yet written. Paul's trumpet is "the trump of God" that gathers His people (1 Thess. 4:16). The trumpets in Revelation are trumpets of judgment blown by angels. In context, "last" is best read as the trumpet that closes the church age.

qa.q: Doesn't 2 Thessalonians 2:3 say that the falling away and the man of sin must come "first"?

a.p: The "day" Paul speaks of is not the rapture but "the day of the Lord," the day of judgment. The Thessalonian believers had been shaken by the idea that they were already in that day. Paul corrects them: that day has not yet come, and when it comes, the falling away and the revealing of the man of sin will accompany it. Then verse 7 says that before the man of sin is revealed, "he who now letteth" will first be taken out of the way.[^8]

qa.q: Aren't the people in white robes who "came out of great tribulation" (Rev. 7:14) the church?

a.p: They are most naturally understood as those who believed and were martyred during the Tribulation. John does not recognize them, and the elder has to explain, "These are they which came out of great tribulation" (vv. 13–14). God does not shut the door of salvation after the rapture. This multitude is a testimony of grace: even in the Tribulation, people beyond counting will receive the gospel.

qa.q: "The first resurrection" (Rev. 20:5–6) comes after the Tribulation. Doesn't the rapture happen then too?

a.p: "The first resurrection" refers to a kind of resurrection, the resurrection of life (John 5:29), not a single event on a single day. Christ rose as the firstfruits; afterward "they that are Christ's at his coming" (1 Cor. 15:23). This resurrection comes in an order. Both the believers raised at the rapture and the martyrs of the Tribulation belong to "the first resurrection," so Revelation 20 can be read as showing its final stage.[^9]

qa.q: I have heard that the pretribulation rapture first appeared in the 1830s, or that the Jesuits invented it. Is that true?

a.p: First, the historical facts. The sixteenth-century Jesuit scholar Francisco Ribera taught a "futurist" reading of Revelation, but he did not teach a pretribulation rapture. The claim that it began with a vision of Margaret MacDonald in Scotland in 1830 is also judged weak by scholars.[^10] On the contrary, earlier writings have been brought to light, such as the 1788 work of the American Baptist minister Morgan Edwards.[^11]

There is a more important principle. When a doctrine was first clearly stated does not decide whether it is true. Justification by faith was also recovered at the Reformation. The only standard is Scripture. Like the Bereans, we search the Scriptures to see "whether those things were so" (Acts 17:11).

qa.q: Isn't the word "rapture" absent from the Bible?

a.p: The word "Trinity" does not appear in the Bible, yet the truth runs through all of Scripture. The rapture is similar. It is a single theological term for being "caught up" (harpazō) in 1 Thessalonians 4:17. The same Greek verb is used when the Spirit of the Lord "caught away" Philip (Acts 8:39) and when Paul was "caught up" to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2).

qa.q: If you believe in a pretribulation rapture, won't you grow spiritually careless, thinking "He will take us anyway"?

a.p: Scripture says the opposite: "every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure" (1 John 3:3). Believing that He may come at any time keeps us awake every day. It is rather the thought "there are still seven years of signs to come" that can make the heart slack. Titus teaches that those who look for the blessed hope live "soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world" (Titus 2:12–13).

qa.q: Can we know the date of the rapture?

a.p: No. Bible Insight opposes every attempt to set dates. Every date-setting prediction in history has failed, and each time the church has been deeply wounded.[^12]

qa.q: Does this mean there are two Second Comings?

a.p: There is one Second Coming, but it unfolds in two phases. The First Coming was also one coming made up of many events, from the birth in Bethlehem to the cross, the resurrection and the ascension. In the same way, the coming in the air for His saints and the coming to the earth with His saints together make up one return.

qa.q: Does this mean Christians will not suffer?

a.p: No. The Lord said, "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer" (John 16:33). Believers face persecution and trials even now. What the pretribulation view teaches is that the church will be delivered from the final seven years in which God's wrath is poured out on the earth. It does not mean believers will have no hardship in this world.

qa.q: How should we treat churches and believers who hold another view?

a.p: We honor them as brothers and sisters waiting for the same Lord. The timing of the rapture is not a condition of salvation; it is a difference of interpretation within historic orthodox faith. It is enough to open the text together and talk humbly. We do not divide churches or condemn others over this question.

qa.q: Is "the mark of the beast" a vaccine or a microchip?

a.p: We do not identify any particular product or technology as the mark of the beast. The mark in Revelation 13 is a matter of confession: worshiping the beast and pledging loyalty to its name (Rev. 14:9–11). It is not something a person receives without knowing it. Interpretations that spread fear are not the way of the gospel.

Three things. First, watch and pray (Luke 21:36). Second, live a holy life, purifying ourselves as He is pure (1 John 3:3). Third, share the gospel with neighbors who do not yet know Christ (2 Pet. 3:9). The rapture is not an escape plan; it is a hope. People with hope live today more faithfully.

body.p: After describing the rapture, Paul ends with these words: "Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thess. 4:18). The purpose of this teaching is not argument but comfort: the comfort of meeting again those who have fallen asleep, the comfort of being appointed not to wrath but to salvation, and above all the comfort that "so shall we ever be with the Lord."
Until the day He comes again, let us keep watch and walk together. Maranatha.

notes: W. Bauer, F. W. Danker et al., A Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament (BDAG), 3rd ed., s.v. "ἁρπάζω." The verb describes a sudden removal by a force that cannot be resisted. See also Acts 8:39; 2 Cor. 12:2, 4; Rev. 12:5.

The "seventy weeks" of Daniel 9:24–27 are understood as seventy sevens of years, or 490 years. The sixty-nine weeks end when the Messiah is "cut off" (9:26), and the final week of seven years is taken as a period still in the future. Most premillennialists share this framework. See the chapter on Daniel's seventy weeks in J. D. Pentecost, Things to Come.

The main arguments of each view and their critiques of one another are gathered in one volume in Alan Hultberg, ed., Three Views on the Rapture (2010). Because a scholar of each view writes his own case and responds to the others, it is widely used as a fair comparison.

Imminence does not mean "certainly soon." It means "able to happen at any time, without any other prophesied event needing to occur first." The same expectation appears in 1 Cor. 1:7; Phil. 3:20; James 5:8–9; Rev. 22:20. See R. L. Mayhue, "Why a Pretribulational Rapture?" (2002).

On tēreō ek, J. L. Townsend (1980) and T. R. Edgar (1982) understand it as "keeping outside" the hour of trial, while R. H. Gundry (1973) reads it as "protecting within the trial and bringing out at the end." The same expression appears in John 17:15 ("keep them from the evil"). Townsend argues that it means keeping a person outside the evil one's influence, not protecting him inside it, and cites it as support for the "keeping outside" sense of Rev. 3:10. Because the verse is debated, we do not rest the case on it alone but read it together with lines ②, ④ and ⑦.

The word "church" (ἐκκλησία) occurs nineteen times in Revelation 1–3 and again in 22:16, but not in the earthly scenes of chapters 4–19. Because this is an argument from silence, it is offered only as a supporting observation, not as independent proof.

On the audience and setting of Matthew 24 (v. 15 "the holy place," v. 16 "them which be in Judaea," v. 20 "the sabbath day"), see the relevant chapter of Walvoord, The Rapture Question (rev. ed., 1979). The posttribulational reading is found in Ladd, The Blessed Hope (1956).

A minority view reads "falling away" (ἀποστασία) in 2 Thess. 2:3 as a "departure," that is, the rapture itself. This section keeps the usual meaning, "apostasy," and rests the argument on "he who now letteth" in vv. 6–7. For a comparison of the view that the restrainer is the restraining work of the Holy Spirit with other views, see the discussion of the restrainer in Pentecost, Things to Come.

The three stages of the first resurrection (Christ → the church at the rapture → the Tribulation martyrs) are explained with a chart in the Bible Insight lecture "Three Distinctions in the First Resurrection" (Korean).

T. D. Ice, "Why the Doctrine of the Pretribulational Rapture Did Not Begin with Margaret Macdonald," Bibliotheca Sacra 147 (1990): 155–168. Even some posttribulational scholars do not accept the MacDonald-origin theory.

Morgan Edwards, Two Academical Exercises on Subjects Bearing the Following Titles: Millennium, Last-Novelties (Philadelphia, 1788). An early medieval sermon handed down under the name of the fourth-century Syrian father Ephraem (often called "Pseudo-Ephraem") is also frequently cited (Demy and Ice, 1995). Its interpretation is debated among scholars, so it is mentioned here only as a source under discussion.

In a 2010 survey by the Pew Research Center, 41 percent of Americans said Christ will return to earth by 2050. Belief in the Second Coming is widespread, and for that reason date-setting claims do great harm to the church when they arise.
